design_detail: Single-author mixed-methods study of online news about mephedrone in the UK during the 2009–2010 'drug scare' that preceded the ban (enforced 16 April 2010). Quantitative parts: (1) screenshots of Google Trends and Google Insights (Figs 1–6, generated 25/02/10, 17/03/10, 22/03/10, 24/03/10 and 06/09/10) showing the normalised volume of Google web searches for 'mephedrone' and 'mephedrone buy' (and, in Fig. 5, 'mephedrone deaths') with Google's news reference volume, read for the timing of news and searches; (2) a case series of the 18 alleged mephedrone deaths of named individuals that Google News returned from 26/11/09 until one year after the ban (suicides and accidental or violent deaths excluded), each with the number of web pages Google Advanced Search returned for the name with 'mephedrone' on 23/06/11, age, sex, place, date first named online, other drugs and causes as alleged in the press, and mephedrone's toxicological status as later reported (Table 1). Qualitative part: all online news about mephedrone over the period was read in date order, themes were identified and illustrative quotations extracted from news items, politicians' statements and posts on an online drug forum; no coding frame, second coder or analytic procedure is described. The quantitative part is appraised below; the qualitative part is described. No statistics.
can_establish: Which deaths of named people were linked to mephedrone in online news from November 2009 to about April 2011, how many web pages linked each name to the drug by June 2011, and what later press reports of inquests said about mephedrone in them: of 18, mephedrone was later reported undetected in 4 (including the two most linked), present but not a factor in 4, and a factor in 7, and one early death was reported as natural causes; and that relative Google search interest in mephedrone, and in 'mephedrone buy', rose around the most-reported deaths.
cannot_establish: Whether news of deaths made more people seek or buy mephedrone (the search data are normalised screenshots without absolute numbers, controls or tests, and a search is not a purchase); how many mephedrone-related deaths occurred (only deaths named in online news, with suicides and violent deaths excluded); whether the toxicology classifications are right (they come from press reports of inquests, not from records); or that the Internet itself accelerated and inflated the scare (no comparison with news before the Internet).

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: deaths of named individuals attributed to mephedrone in online news that Google News returned for 'mephedrone' between 26/11/09 and one year after the ban (p. 200, Methods, 2nd paragraph; p. 203). Google states that its news aggregator watches 4500 English-language news sites; its full source list is not public (p. 200).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Alleged mephedrone deaths of named people in online news; Table 1 excludes suicides and accidental or violent deaths linked to mephedrone (Table 1 notes, p. 204). How many deaths were excluded, and who classed them, is not stated.
sample.demographics: Ages 14 to 49; 10 women and 8 men; 9 of the 18 aged 14–19 (editors' count from Table 1, consistent with the text's statement that half were teenagers and most were female, p. 203). Places in England, Scotland (Ayr, Fife) and Northern Ireland (Table 1, p. 204).
sample.selection_effects: The 18 are the media's selection, which is the object of study, not a sample of mephedrone-related deaths: only deaths that online news named and Google News indexed, from undisclosed sources returned by Google's own parameters; unnamed deaths, deaths not reported online, suicides and violent deaths are absent.

exposure.measurement: For the deaths: other drug use and other causes as alleged in the press, and mephedrone's status as subsequently reported in Table 1 notes a–c. The text quotes newspaper inquest reports and also cites Dargan and Wood's 2011 technical report for confirmed cases; the table does not identify a source for each classification. No original coroners' records, toxicology reports or concentrations are presented. For searches: normalised Google indices give relative rather than absolute numbers (p. 200).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; amounts are not reported as data.
exposure.polysubstance: Other substances or conditions as alleged in the press (Table 1, p. 204): alcohol and methadone (#1, #2, #14); ketamine, in brackets (#3); antidepressants with a heart condition (#5); intravenous use with heart disease, HIV, diabetes, kidney disease and high blood pressure (#6); alcohol (#7; 'spiked' alcohol #10); amphetamine, BZP and TFMPP (#9); morphine (#11); amphetamine (#12); alcohol, GHB and diazepam (#13); morphine and ketamine (#15); cannabis with failure to use seizure medication (#16); 'underlying health problems' (#17); a 'drug cocktail' (#18). None for #4 and #8.

comparison.controls: None for the deaths. Implicit comparisons: online attention, before the ban, to deaths later found not to be caused by mephedrone, against attention, after the ban, to toxicologically confirmed deaths; local against national newspaper coverage of the same inquests (qualitative); and a cited Office for National Statistics count (6 toxicologically confirmed drug-related deaths involving mephedrone in England and Wales in 2010, p. 205), not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: Google Trends and Google Insights search volume index and news reference volume (screenshots, Figs 1–6); estimated number of web pages returned by Google Advanced Search for 'mephedrone AND [deceased's name]' on 23/06/11 (Table 1); date first named online; qualitative reading of news items and forum posts.
outcomes.validity_norms: The notes to Table 1 state that the retrieval counts measure only the linkage of a name to mephedrone, not the strength of the link or the traffic or coverage a case received (p. 204). Google Trends values are relative, of limited graphic resolution, and depend on search terms and spellings (p. 200).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Newsworthiness' is the number of web pages (not only news, and including pages that refuted the link) returned for the name with 'mephedrone' on a single day, 23/06/11. A 'false alarm' is a death in which mephedrone was later reported undetected or not a factor, or a death reported as due to natural causes, according to the press.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; single author, no second coder.

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics. Editors' tally of the Table 1 notes: mephedrone later reported undetected in 4 of 18 (#1, #2, #4, #14), present but not a factor in 4 (#7, #11, #15, #16), a cause-of-death factor in 7 (#5, #6, #8, #9, #10, #12, #13), and no note in 3 (#3, reported in the text as natural causes; #17; #18). The two deaths with most retrievals (9060 and 8730, the two Scunthorpe deaths) and the fourth (2040) were among the undetected; the third (2490) is the death reported as natural causes. Editors' calculation: the 4 undetected deaths account for 20,133 of the 31,238 retrievals for all 18 (64%), the 7 'factor' deaths for 6,186 (20%); 9 of 18 (50%, Wilson 95% interval 29% to 71%) were later reported as not caused by mephedrone. The text reports that searches doubled after the first death report and trebled within days of the Scunthorpe story (pp. 201–202), from screenshots without absolute search counts.
analysis.selective_reporting: Quotations were chosen by the author as illustrative, without a stated sampling rule; the excluded deaths (suicides, accidental or violent deaths) are neither listed nor counted; the screenshots were generated on five dates and are not complete time series.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 18 named deaths linked to mephedrone in online news, Table 1 marks 4 as later reported undetected, 4 as detected but not a cause-of-death factor, 7 as a factor and 3 without a toxicology note. One of the last 3 is described in the text as natural causes: 9 of 18 were therefore later reported not caused by mephedrone. The three cases with most name-linked web pages were among these 9. Six of the 7 factor cases had other drugs or illnesses alleged; a factor need not be the sole or main cause. Relative searches for 'mephedrone' and 'mephedrone buy' rose around highly reported deaths. Only the general 'mephedrone' series extends beyond the ban and shows a later fall; buying-search screenshots end on 22 and 24 March 2010, before the 16 April ban. These observations do not establish that news caused purchases or use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says "The fatalities which received the most Internet traffic subsequently proved false-alarms" (p. 198), while the notes to Table 1 say the retrieval counts do not measure traffic or coverage (p. 204). The text says the data would support the hypothesis that reports of deaths caused by a drug increase interest in buying it, and that Figs 1–6 suggest a 'boomerang effect', news of drug deaths causing more interest in the drug (p. 205); the evidence is co-occurrence in normalised screenshots, the author concedes that a search is not a purchase and that Google Trends show neither numbers nor reasons (p. 205), and the Fig. 5 screenshot itself says 'mephedrone deaths' had too little search volume for ranking. The conclusion that the Internet accelerated and inflated the scare has no comparison with a scare before online news. The statement that coverage confirming mephedrone was not responsible was much smaller than earlier speculation (p. 203) rests on the news-volume line in Fig. 6, which does not show what the news said. The empirical core, that several of the most-linked alleged deaths were later reported not to involve mephedrone causally, is supported by Table 1 as described, with second-hand toxicology.

timeline.event: Forsyth's earlier quantitative study of drug-fatality reports in the popular press ('Distorted?'), cited here; not in PubMed according to the project's search log, not read.
This study: 18 alleged mephedrone deaths named in online news, followed to later press reports of inquests.
Schifano et al.: of 128 alleged mephedrone-associated deaths in the UK national register, mephedrone was not found at post-mortem in 25 (card sc_schifano_2012).

Sumnall et al.: randomized online experiment on how a news report's depiction of a person who died after drug use (gender, age and use history, drug) affects public stigma and support for harm reduction (card sc_sumnall_2023).

replication.where_it_stands: No repetition of the method for another drug scare is reported in the paper. Its central factual point agrees with the national register series of Schifano et al. (2012), which found mephedrone absent at post-mortem in 25 of 128 alleged deaths, but the toxicology here is second-hand from newspapers. The project's drug-deaths list found no other study comparing press reports of individual drug deaths with later inquest or toxicology findings beyond the mephedrone episode (search-logs/DrugDeaths_DOI-LIST.md, section 6, Known gaps).

what_would_settle_it: Link every death attributed to a new drug in news reports over a defined period to the coroner's or pathologist's records (toxicology with concentrations, cause and manner of death), and measure with absolute data (search counts, sales, test purchases or repeated surveys) and a comparison drug or period whether reports of deaths are followed by changes in use.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist for the quantitative case series, as the round brief directs for mixed-methods studies and for case series without a comparison; the qualitative part (chronological reading of all online news, themes and illustrative quotations from newspapers, politicians and forum posts) is described, not appraised: it reports no coding frame, second coder, reflexivity or ethics review. The editors summarise the risk of bias as high because death classifications are second-hand, with newspaper accounts and a technical report cited but no source named for each table entry and the search data are relative screenshots. The study may be cited for (as second-hand reporting, without implying sole or main cause): the 18 named deaths linked to mephedrone in online news and what later press reports of inquests said about mephedrone in them (4 undetected, 4 not a factor, 1 natural causes, 7 a factor), with the caveat that this toxicology is second-hand; for the observation that the deaths with most web pages linking them to mephedrone were among those it did not cause; for relative search interest rising around the most-reported deaths, as a description; and, as cited from ONS, 6 toxicologically confirmed mephedrone deaths in England and Wales in 2010, 2 with mephedrone alone. It may not be cited for news causing searches, purchases or use, for counts of mephedrone deaths, or for effects of the Internet on drug scares in general.

key_findings.finding: Methods: Google Trends produced time-trend graphs of searches for 'mephedrone' with Google's news reference volume, links to headlines, the countries and cities searches came from and related terms; Google Insights compared search terms (e.g. 'mephedrone death' with 'mephedrone buy'). Google News was used to read in date order all online news about mephedrone from 26/11/09, the start of the scare, until one year after the ban, to identify themes and extract illustrative quotations, and to identify all UK mephedrone deaths reported online; Google Advanced Search then quantified online activity for each death ('Mephedrone AND [deceased's name]').
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations of the Google tools as stated: one search engine; Google News returns stories only from sources it selects (its full list is not public; Google says the aggregator watches 4500 English-language news sites); Google Trends values are normalised, giving the relative number of searches as a proportion of the highest volume rather than absolute numbers, at limited graphic resolution; counts depend on spellings and nicknames. The author treats the relative timing of news and searches as more important than the numbers.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Google News searches from 26/11/09 until one year after the ban retrieved 18 alleged mephedrone deaths of named individuals, listed in Table 1 by the estimated number of web articles Google Advanced Search returned for the name with 'mephedrone' (searched 23/06/11). Table 1 excludes suicides and accidental or violent deaths linked to mephedrone; its notes say the counts measure only the linkage of the name to mephedrone, not the strength of the link or the traffic or coverage a case received.
key_findings.locator: Findings › Measuring newsworthy drug-related deaths from online media, 1st paragraph (p. 203); Table 1 and its notes (p. 204)

key_findings.finding: Later toxicology as reported (Table 1 notes): mephedrone undetected in 4 deaths (#1 and #2, men aged 18 and 19 in Scunthorpe, 9060 and 8730 retrievals; #4, a woman aged 17 in Cumbria, 2040; #14, a woman aged 18 in Newcastle, 303); detected but not a factor in 4 (#7, #11, #15, #16; 1710, 457, 243 and 8 retrievals); detected and a cause-of-death factor in 7 (#5, #6, #8, #9, #10, #12, #13; 310 to 1860 retrievals), 6 of them with other drugs or conditions alleged; no note in 3 (#3, a girl aged 14 in Brighton and Hove, 2490 retrievals, with streptococcal A infection listed among other causes; #17; #18).
key_findings.locator: Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' tally of Table 1 note letters: 4 undetected, 4 detected but not a factor, 7 factors, 3 without a note. The notes say subsequently reported and do not identify a source case by case. The text quotes newspaper inquest accounts and also cites Dargan and Wood (2011), not independently read here. For case #6, the quoted pathologist considered mephedrone alone unlikely to explain death given severe coronary disease; footnote 8 reports a later amendment attributing a contributory role. A factor does not mean sole or main cause.

key_findings.finding: Half of the 18 were teenagers and most were female, in line with research on the 1990s ecstasy scare; a 46-year-old man had the 6th highest count; his death at first had a single Google News return, from his local paper, and was not reported online again until the day the Scunthorpe story broke, when it was presented as the first toxicologically confirmed mephedrone death.
key_findings.locator: Findings › Measuring newsworthy drug-related deaths from online media, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 1: 9 aged 14–19; 10 women, 8 men.

key_findings.finding: The first death linked to mephedrone in the press (a 14-year-old girl, November 2009) was reported within a month, in local online newspapers, as due to natural causes (bronchopneumonia after a streptococcal A infection, according to the pathologist's report as quoted); earlier accounts blaming mephedrone stayed online, and local, national and international titles went on naming her as a mephedrone death for months.
key_findings.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 3rd and 4th paragraphs and the quotations after them (indented quotations not counted as paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: On 16–17 March 2010 a story attributed the deaths of two teenage men in Scunthorpe to mephedrone; press campaigns for a ban followed, citing links between mephedrone and a 'string of deaths' without toxicological confirmation, and the drug was banned (enforced 16/04/10). One month after the ban (18/05/10) it was reported that the two had not used mephedrone; an inquest in 2011 found they died from a combination of alcohol and methadone.
key_findings.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 8th paragraph (p. 201) and 10th, 13th and 14th paragraphs (p. 202)

key_findings.finding: The author reads the screenshots as showing general mephedrone searches rising after the first reported death and trebling after the Scunthorpe story, alongside increased news (Figs 1–3). Buying searches also rose (Fig. 4, generated 22 March 2010). He describes Fig. 5 (24 March) as showing buying and death-search spikes together, but the displayed search panel contains only the buying line and states that the death term has insufficient volume for ranking. The post-ban fall shown in Fig. 6 (6 September) concerns general 'mephedrone' searches and news, with no post-ban buying-search series.
key_findings.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 1st, 9th and 12th paragraphs; Figs 1–6
key_findings.note: Values not extracted: the figures are screenshots of normalised indices without absolute numbers. The Fig. 5 screenshot (300-dpi crop) states that 'mephedrone deaths' did not have enough search volume for ranking and shows one clearly visible line.

key_findings.finding: The author concedes that entering 'mephedrone buy' does not mean a person intended to buy, or started using the drug because of the coverage, and that Google Trends show neither how many searched nor why; he nonetheless reads Figs 1–6 as suggesting a 'boomerang effect', news of drug deaths causing more interest in the drug, including buying it.
key_findings.locator: Implications › Do media false-alarms lead to real harms?, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cited from the Office for National Statistics (2011): six toxicologically confirmed drug-related deaths involving mephedrone were recorded in England and Wales in 2010, out of a total of 2747 drug-related deaths, and in two of them mephedrone was the only drug recorded or detected.
key_findings.locator: Implications › Do media false-alarms lead to real harms?, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures as Forsyth reports them. His ONS reference is a 2011 report about deaths related to drug poisoning in England and Wales in 2010 (p. 208); the report itself was not read, so its definition and occurrence/registration basis are not established here.

key_findings.finding: The author says later coverage clearing mephedrone was smaller than earlier speculation and that cases implicated at inquest received less coverage. Fig. 6 shows news volume, not the contents of that news, so this distinction is his reading rather than a separate coded comparison. For the Berkhamsted case #11, the quoted national report centres mephedrone, while the quoted local inquest report omits it and gives more detail of the causes. The author interprets local titles as more likely to discuss alcohol, medicines and social circumstances.
key_findings.locator: Findings › Measuring the time-line of a virtual drug scare, 15th paragraph (p. 203); Findings › Measuring newsworthy drug-related deaths from online media, 7th paragraph (pp. 204–205); Has the Internet impacted on drug news?, 1st paragraph (p. 206)

key_findings.finding: Posts on an online drug forum by people who said they knew the deceased gave accounts of other drugs, intravenous use and earlier mephedrone use in two deaths (Hove and Berkhamsted) before the inquests, which later inquest reports corroborated in part; the author presents this as reader-generated information contesting stock drug-scare stories.
key_findings.locator: Findings › Measuring newsworthy drug-related deaths from online media, 3rd, 4th, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: An alleged death later classed as a false alarm (#4, Cumbria) was followed, according to a magazine source, by local police prioritising mephedrone and a ten-fold increase in drug arrests involving people who use cannabis at a summer 2010 music festival. Table 1 dates the first naming to 19 April 2010, after the 16 April ban; the text incorrectly calls it the day after the ban.
key_findings.locator: Implications › Do media false-alarms lead to real harms?, 4th paragraph (p. 205) and the quotation that follows (p. 206)
key_findings.note: Second-hand (Power, 2011, Mixmag); not verified in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the deaths with the most Internet traffic proved false alarms, but the notes to Table 1 say the retrieval counts are not a measure of traffic or coverage.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's claim should be read as the most web pages linking the name to mephedrone on 23/06/11, a cumulative count that includes pages refuting the link.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 18 alleged mephedrone deaths were identified from online news, without saying that Table 1 excludes suicides and accidental or violent deaths linked to mephedrone, whose number is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 18 are not all deaths alleged in online news to involve mephedrone; the share of false alarms applies to this subset.

reporting_issues.issue: Dates conflict internally: a Metro front page is dated 17 March 2011 for the March 2010 Scunthorpe story; New Zealand Herald and Epoch Times dates are March 2011 in the text but March 2010 in the references; Drink & Drug News is January 2004 in the text but January 2010 in the list. Text dates for Guardian items (March and May 2011) differ from the 2010 references, and an Observer item dated March 2011 corresponds to a June 2010 reference. Figure captions place an NME item in September 2010 on earlier graphs. The stated search/scare start is 26 November 2009 in Methods but 24 November elsewhere and for Table 1 case #3. The Cumbria case is called the day after the ban, although its table date is 19 April and the ban date is 16 April 2010.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dates in the text cannot be used without checking the reference list; the key sequence (ban enforced 16/04/10, Scunthorpe deaths reported as mephedrone-free 18/05/10, inquest 2011) is consistent throughout.

reporting_issues.issue: The author describes Fig. 5 as simultaneous buying and death-search spikes. The search panel instead displays the red buying line and an insufficient-volume warning for the death term; the blue line below is news volume, not a second search series.
reporting_issues.consequence: The co-occurrence of searches about deaths and about buying cannot be checked from the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists case #15 (Berkhamsted, woman, morphine and ketamine, first named online 19/10/10) as aged 26, while the press reports quoted on pp. 204–205 give 28 for the woman who died after the same Berkhamsted party, the only other Berkhamsted case.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one age in Table 1 is probably wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Fig. 1 explains markers A and B, but the screenshot carries markers A to E.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three of the news events marked on the first graph cannot be identified.

design_detail: Brief report: a descriptive case series of deaths in the UK, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man that were alleged to be associated with mephedrone (4-methylmethcathinone), from the first known UK death in September 2009 to np-SAD forms received by 31 October 2011. Cases came mainly from the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (np-SAD) database at St George's, University of London, which receives coroners' information on drug-related deaths, and also from Internet searches of toxicological, newspaper and other media websites and from canvassing members of the London Toxicology Group; media reports were also used to fill in np-SAD's data collection form where the full coronial file could not be accessed (Methods, pp. 710–711). Of 128 alleged deaths, the 62 'confirmed' deaths (mephedrone identified, inquest concluded, form received) are described: sociodemographics, verdicts, circumstances grouped by the authors into six categories (Table 1), other substances found (Table 2), and mephedrone concentrations (quantified in 38). Figure 1 plots three monthly series (suspected deaths, deaths with confirmed mephedrone intake, confirmed deaths 'caused or contributed to' by mephedrone), July 2009 to August 2011. Descriptive only, with one t-test (age by sex); no comparison group and no denominator of people using mephedrone. Two authors are at St George's International Centre for Drug Policy, which publishes np-SAD's annual report (reference 20).
can_establish: What had been recorded by October 2011 about deaths in the UK and Islands in which mephedrone was alleged or found: how many alleged deaths had no mephedrone at post-mortem (25 of 128) or were awaiting toxicology (13), and, for 62 concluded inquests with mephedrone identified, the recorded verdicts, the circumstances as the authors grouped them, the other substances found, and the mephedrone concentrations measured in 38.
cannot_establish: That mephedrone caused or contributed to these deaths (the case definition is presence, and other substances were found in 54 of the 62, an editors' calculation: 62 minus the 8 with mephedrone alone); the risk of dying after using mephedrone or how it compares with other drugs (no denominator, as the authors state); that mephedrone caused the self-harm or risky behaviour (no psychiatric histories, no comparison group); or what concentration is dangerous (the specimen is named only as blood after death, and no sampling site, interval after death or comparison with deaths from other causes or with living people is reported).

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: deaths notified to np-SAD by coroners (England and Wales, Northern Ireland, the Islands) and procurators fiscal (Scotland), with information since 2004 also from the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency and the General Register Office for Northern Ireland; plus cases found through Internet searches of toxicological, newspaper and other media sites and by canvassing the London Toxicology Group (pp. 710–711). np-SAD records a drug-related death if at least one of three criteria is met: one or more psychoactive substances directly implicated in the death; a 'history of dependence or abuse of drugs'; controlled drugs present at post-mortem (p. 710). About 95% of coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly, and the authors call the counts a minimum (p. 710).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: The Results describe the analysed ('confirmed') deaths as those with mephedrone identified at post-mortem, a concluded inquest and an np-SAD form received by 31 October 2011 (p. 711). Table 2's footnote says one of the 62, who died in hospital 3 weeks after taking mephedrone, had none identified at post-mortem. An earlier test or history could explain inclusion, but the paper does not report that person's individual confirmation evidence (p. 712). Outside the analysis: 25 alleged deaths with mephedrone not found, 13 with toxicology pending, and 28 of the 90 described as positive (21 with the inquest not concluded, 7 without a form; editors' arithmetic).
sample.demographics: Mean age 28.8 years (SD 11.3; range 14–64); men 29.0 and women 28.0 years on average (t=0.275, not significant), but the number of men and women is not given. Where known, 'most' were described as white (no count). Born in the UK and Islands 41, overseas 7. Unemployed 18, students 11; the number employed is printed as 'Many' with a superscript 24 (reporting issue). 29 known to be dependent on or misusing drugs, 10 not, 23 unknown. 12 were prescribed psychoactive medicines (methadone, diazepam, antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiepileptics, opioid analgesics). 35 died at their own or a friend's home, 5 in hospital. Deaths in England 46, Scotland 9, Northern Ireland 4, Wales 1, Guernsey 2 (p. 711).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 66 of the 128 alleged deaths are outside the analysis (editors' arithmetic: 25 negative, 13 pending, 28 positive without a concluded inquest or a form); whether they differ from the 62 is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Deaths enter by allegation, partly from media reports, and are 'confirmed' by mephedrone being found, so, by construction, deaths in which mephedrone was not tested for, not detected or not alleged are not counted (editors' reading); the authors' own reasons for calling the count a minimum or an underestimate are that 95% of coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly (p. 710), that positive cases await inquest, that tests vary in sensitivity and that geographical coverage is incomplete (p. 713). Deaths whose inquests concluded quickly may be over-represented among the 62. np-SAD's criteria admit a death with a controlled drug present at post-mortem whatever the cause, and the paper does not say which criterion admitted each death, so deaths by hanging, drowning or stabbing can be in the series because a drug was present rather than implicated. The controlled-drug criterion could apply to mephedrone itself only after its classification, which the paper places in spring 2010 (p. 712, Discussion, 2nd paragraph); for the 31 of the 62 deaths dated up to March 2010 by Figure 1's monthly labels (editors' count), mephedrone's presence alone did not meet that criterion (editors' inference from the paper's dates). Some case details came from press reports (p. 711).

exposure.measurement: Toxicology recorded in coronial files and np-SAD forms. Results refer collectively to post-mortem or ante-mortem findings, without identifying individual ante-mortem cases. The Table 2 footnote's post-mortem-negative hospital death is not accompanied by an individual earlier test result. The Discussion calls the concentrations post-mortem blood levels, but blood type, sampling site, interval and laboratory methods or screening panels are not reported. Concentrations were quantified in 38 of the 62 deaths (pp. 711–712). Whether mephedrone was formally included in the cause of death (36 deaths, 18 with mephedrone on its own) comes from the recorded cause; who wrote it and on what evidence is not stated (p. 711).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Amounts taken and routes are not reported for the deaths. Concentrations (one value over 2000 mg/L excluded as an outlier, n=37): mean 1.938 mg/L (range <0.01 to 22.0); 10 'monomephedrone' cases mean 1.996 mg/L (range <0.01 to 12.15); 27 combined cases mean 1.749 mg/L (range 0.03 to 22.0) (pp. 711–712).
exposure.polysubstance: Mephedrone was the only substance found in 8 of the 62 deaths (13%). Other substances found: alcohol 26; stimulants (e.g. amphetamine, methamphetamine, cocaine, MDMA) 22; hypnotics or sedatives (including diazepam, nitrazepam, lorazepam, zopiclone) 22; opiates or opioids (including methadone, buprenorphine, morphine, codeine, dihydrocodeine, oxycodone, and papaverine as printed) 13; piperazines 13; other synthetic cathinones (e.g. MDPV, methylone, flephedrone) 13; antidepressants 8; antipsychotics 5; GBL/GHB 5; cannabis 5; ketamine 2; miscellaneous (including antiepileptics, levamisole, cocaethylene, lignocaine, atropine, hyoscine) 9 (Table 2, p. 712). Which substances occurred together in each death is not tabulated, and other substances enter no analysis; the authors say mephedrone's role in the polydrug deaths remains unclear (p. 712).

comparison.controls: None: no deaths involving other drugs, no deaths from other causes and no living people for comparison. The discussion sets the share of self-harm deaths against suicide rates of 3% to 6% recorded by UK coroners in the authors' larger series on amphetamine-type drugs, MDMA, cocaine and khat (p. 713), without saying whether those series used the same inclusion criteria or the same definition of self-harm.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric history is 'not typically made available' to np-SAD (p. 712): mental-health diagnoses, previous self-harm and most physical illness are unknown (only cardiovascular conditions 3, bronchopneumonia 2 and chronic pain 1 are listed, p. 711), so the self-harm deaths cannot be separated from risk that existed before mephedrone.

outcomes.instruments: Verdict or conclusion of the coroner or procurator fiscal; recorded cause of death (whether mephedrone was formally included); circumstances of death grouped by the authors into six categories (Table 1); substances found at post-mortem (Table 2); place, country and weekday of death; sociodemographics from the files.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. The circumstance categories were assigned by the authors from coronial files and, for some cases, press reports, without stated rules or a second rater.
outcomes.operationalization: A 'confirmed' death means mephedrone was identified, not that it caused the death; the authors state that presence at post-mortem does not necessarily mean mephedrone caused or contributed to death (p. 713). 'Acute drug toxicity after having taken mephedrone' (26 deaths) includes mephedrone taken alone or with other substances (Table 1). Figure 1 plots a separate series of deaths 'caused or contributed to by mephedrone' without saying who decided this or how.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: one test (age by sex); everything else is descriptive.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and percentages only, no intervals. Editors' calculations (Wilson 95% intervals): alleged deaths with mephedrone not found at post-mortem 25 of 128, 19.5% (13.6% to 27.2%), or 25 of the 115 with results, 21.7% (15.2% to 30.1%); mephedrone the only substance found 8 of 62, 12.9% (6.7% to 23.4%); mephedrone in the recorded cause of death 36 of 62, 58.1% (45.7% to 69.5%); self-inflicted harm 18 of 62, 29.0% (19.2% to 41.3%); suicide verdict 11 of 62, 17.7% (10.2% to 29.0%); accident or misadventure verdict 35 of 62, 56.5% (44.1% to 68.1%). The 'nearly triple' weekday contrast (46 deaths Saturday to Tuesday) compares four days with three: if the day was known for all 62, it is 11.5 deaths per day against 5.3, about 2.2 times (editors' calculation). Concentrations are summarised as means of skewed data without medians.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported, though held in the files the authors read: the number of men and women; which substances were found together in each death; the circumstances of the 8 mephedrone-only deaths and their concentrations; the blood type, sampling site and timing for the concentrations; and the data behind the statement that intentional and non-intentional deaths showed no apparent differences (p. 712).
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive). Subgroups are small (8 mephedrone-only deaths; 10 'monomephedrone' concentrations).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 128 deaths alleged by October 2011 to be associated with mephedrone, mephedrone was not found in 25 and results were pending in 13. Of 62 concluded inquests with mephedrone identified, it was the only substance found in 8; it was in the recorded cause of death in 36 (on its own in 18); 18 deaths were self-inflicted (11 by hanging), 6 followed accidents or violence while under the influence, 5 followed collapse at a party, and 26 were acute drug toxicity with mephedrone alone or with other substances. Verdicts: accident or misadventure 35, suicide 11, open 8, 'abuse of drugs' 5, homicide, natural causes and narrative 1 each. There is no denominator and no comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the data "may suggest a significant level of caution when ingesting mephedrone" (p. 710) and describes typical victims as male without giving a count of men. The discussion reads the 8 mephedrone-only deaths as possibly confirming concern about the drug's own acute toxicity (p. 712), though their circumstances and concentrations are not given separately. It raises the possibility that mephedrone causes or worsens psychosis or depression leading to self-harm, supported only by few antipsychotic and antidepressant findings and by 'no apparent differences' between intentional and non-intentional deaths, for which no data are shown (p. 712), and contrasts the 29% self-harm share with 3% to 6% suicide rates in other stimulant series (p. 713), which compares self-harm by any means (including deaths admitted because mephedrone was present) with recorded suicides elsewhere. It says confirmed deaths seemed to fall after the spring 2010 classification process (p. 712), while the limitations add that changes over time may reflect coroners' methods, policies, laws or forensic technology (p. 713). The discussion explains the alleged deaths not related to mephedrone by other drugs being found (p. 712), whereas the results define them by mephedrone not being found, which the limitations note could also reflect test sensitivity. The limitations are otherwise candid: presence does not imply cause, the count is a minimum, and without a death rate the size of the risk cannot be determined (p. 713).

timeline.event: Beynon et al. described np-SAD's wider drug-related-death definition, which counts deaths with a drug history or with controlled drugs present at post-mortem, and what it contained in one city (card sc_beynon_2007).
Schifano et al. counted UK deaths with ketamine mentioned, from the same register and coroners' reports (card sc_schifano_2008, written by another reader).

Earlier reports of mephedrone detected in deaths in Scotland (Torrance & Cooper, 2010) and of mephedrone-related deaths (Maskell et al., 2011), cited by this paper as having described some of the same cases; not read.
This series: 128 alleged UK deaths, 25 mephedrone-negative, 62 confirmed by October 2011.
Forsyth followed 18 alleged mephedrone deaths named in online news: by later press reports of inquests, mephedrone was undetected in 4 and present but not a factor in 4 (card sc_forsyth_2012).

replication.where_it_stands: The paper presents itself as the UK-wide series to October 2011 and asks for similar studies elsewhere; none is reported in it. The project's drug-deaths list found no systematic review re-examining deaths attributed to cathinones (search-logs/DrugDeaths_DOI-LIST.md, section 5, Known gaps). Read with Forsyth (2012), which followed the most publicised of the same alleged deaths through online news and found several were later reported to have no mephedrone or another cause.

funding.funder: No funding statement for this study. A footnote says np-SAD received support from the Department of Health in 2004 to 2010 (p. 710).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest that may have influenced the interpretation of the data, but note: Schifano is a full member of the UK Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ACMD); Corkery is a member of the ACMD New Psychoactive Drugs working group; Ghodse is Chair of the United Nations International Narcotics Control Board (INCB); and Schifano receives funding from the European Commission for the ReDNet project (EC Executive Agency for Health and Consumers, Public Health Programme; 2009 12 26). The views are stated to be the authors' own, not necessarily those of the Department of Health, Home Office, European Commission, ACMD or INCB (p. 713).
funding.affiliations_note: School of Pharmacy, University of Hertfordshire; Hertfordshire Partnership NHS Foundation Trust; International Centre for Drug Policy, St George's University of London, where the np-SAD database is held (p. 710). Two authors sat on the ACMD, whose 2010 consideration of the cathinones the paper cites; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount the counts.

what_would_settle_it: A complete national series of deaths in which mephedrone was tested for, with standard toxicology (named specimen, sampling site and interval after death), cause and manner of death decided by pathologists blind to any allegation, and an explicit rule for classing mephedrone as causal, contributory or incidental; the same rules applied to deaths involving other stimulants, and survey estimates of the number of people using mephedrone to give a death rate.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: For deaths with mephedrone present in the UK, a coroner-fed national register plus media and toxicologists' reports is a reasonable frame, but entry depends on an allegation and on coroners reporting (95% of coroners' areas in England and Wales; no figure for Scotland or Northern Ireland).
All identified cases were sought, but the analysis is restricted to deaths with concluded inquests and returned forms (62 of the 90 positives).
62 deaths; the proportions carry wide intervals (self-harm 29.0%, 19.2% to 41.3%, editors' calculation) and key subgroups are small (8 mephedrone-only deaths).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, birthplace, verdicts, circumstances, place and substances are given, but not the number of men and women, the number employed (garbled), or which substances occurred together, and concentrations are not linked to circumstances.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 28 of the 90 mephedrone-positive deaths (31%) and the 13 pending cases are not analysed, and no comparison with the analysed deaths is reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Mephedrone's presence is the case definition, but laboratories, methods and screening panels are not described. The Discussion names blood for the concentrations without giving blood type, sampling site or timing. One 'confirmed' case had no mephedrone at post-mortem, with individual confirmation evidence unstated; whether mephedrone caused or contributed is not decided by any stated rule.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Toxicology from different coroners' laboratories with unknown panels; concentrations in 38 of 62; some details supplemented from press reports; circumstance categories assigned by the authors without stated rules.

Counts suit a case series, but no intervals are given, the overall mean concentration does not match its subgroup means, means are given for skewed concentrations without medians, and the weekday contrast compares four days with three.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: About 95% of coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly; 7 concluded inquests had no form returned; completeness elsewhere in the UK is not given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison. The series is assembled by allegation, analysed only for concluded inquests, measured with undescribed and non-standard toxicology, and classifies mephedrone's role by presence, so the editors summarise the risk of bias as high for any statement about how many deaths mephedrone caused. As a record of what was alleged and found it is useful and the authors' limitations are candid. It may be cited for: the counts of alleged, negative, pending and confirmed deaths to October 2011 (25 of 128 alleged deaths mephedrone-negative); the verdicts, circumstances and other substances recorded in the 62; mephedrone being the only substance found in 8; the concentration ranges as printed, with their missing blood type, sampling site and timing; and the authors' statement that presence does not imply cause. It may not be cited for the number of deaths caused by mephedrone, a death rate, a comparison of risk with other drugs, a dangerous concentration, mephedrone causing self-harm, or any combination being especially harmful.

key_findings.finding: Sources and case definition: np-SAD has received coroners' information on drug-related deaths in the UK, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man since 1997 (and since 2004 also from the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency and the General Register Office for Northern Ireland), some 25,000 deaths in all; most (95%) coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly, so the counts are a minimum. A death is recorded if a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, there was a history of dependence or drug misuse, or controlled drugs were present at post-mortem. Further cases came from Internet searches of toxicological, newspaper and media websites and from the London Toxicology Group; media reports supplemented the data collection form where coronial files could not be accessed. Cases with forms received by 31 October 2011 were analysed.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st (only) paragraph (p. 710, right column, continuing on p. 711, left column)

key_findings.finding: Of 128 alleged mephedrone-associated deaths, mephedrone was not found at post-mortem in 25 and toxicology was still pending in 13; of the 90 in which it was identified, inquests had concluded in 69 and forms had been received for 62, which were treated as confirmed fatalities and analysed.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract (p. 710) gives 128, 90, 69 and 62 but not the 25 negative or 13 pending deaths. Editors' calculation: 25 of 128 is 19.5% (Wilson 95% interval 13.6% to 27.2%), or 25 of the 115 with results 21.7% (15.2% to 30.1%).

key_findings.finding: The 62 confirmed deaths: mean age 28.8 years (SD 11.3; range 14–64); mean age 29.0 in men and 28.0 in women (t=0.275, not significant), numbers of each not given; 41 born in the UK and Islands, 7 overseas; 18 unemployed, 11 students; 29 known to be dependent on or misusing drugs, 10 not, 23 unknown; 12 prescribed psychoactive medicines; 35 died at their own or a friend's home and 5 in hospital.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Verdicts or conclusions of coroners or procurators fiscal: accidental death or misadventure 35, 'abuse of drugs' 5, suicide 11, open 8, homicide 1, natural causes 1, narrative 1. Deaths occurred in England 46, Scotland 9, Northern Ireland 4, Wales 1 and Guernsey 2.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The first known UK death was in September 2009; confirmed deaths rose through the first quarter of 2010 with a further peak in July 2010, and the most recent was in May 2011. 46 deaths occurred on Saturdays to Tuesdays, described as nearly triple the number on the other days.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the printed monthly labels in Figure 1 (500-dpi crop): the confirmed-intake series sums to 62, with peaks of 9 in March 2010 and 7 in July 2010; the series 'caused or contributed to by mephedrone' sums to 35, with 29 deaths from September 2009 to June 2010 and 6 from November 2010 to May 2011. Editors' calculation for the weekdays: 11.5 deaths per day on the four days against 5.3 on the other three, about 2.2 times, if the day was known for all 62.

key_findings.finding: Circumstances as grouped by the authors: acute drug toxicity after mephedrone alone or with other psychoactive substances 26; self-inflicted harm 18 (hanging in 11; others by cutting the throat, gunshot, jumping from a bridge or intentional overdose); bizarre or risky behaviour while on mephedrone 6 (drowning after trying to swim across a river, driving under the influence, being stabbed); collapse at a party 5 (a raised temperature while clubbing recorded in 1); death in hospital days or weeks later 5 (3 from acute liver or multi-organ failure); risky sexual activity 2. Pre-existing conditions recorded occasionally: cardiovascular 3, bronchopneumonia 2, chronic pain 1.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 711); Table 1 (p. 712)
key_findings.note: The six categories of Table 1 sum to 62 (editors' check).

key_findings.finding: Mephedrone was formally included in the cause of death in 36 of the 62 deaths, on its own in 18; by post-mortem or ante-mortem results it was the only substance found in 8 (13%). Other substances: alcohol 26, stimulants 22, hypnotics or sedatives 22, opiates or opioids 13, piperazines 13, other synthetic cathinones 13, antidepressants 8, antipsychotics 5, GBL/GHB 5, cannabis 5, ketamine 2, miscellaneous 9 (including levamisole and cocaethylene).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 711); Table 2 (p. 712)
key_findings.note: Who decided the cause of death, and how, is not stated. Editors' calculation: 36 of 62 is 58.1% (Wilson 95% interval 45.7% to 69.5%); 8 of 62 is 12.9% (6.7% to 23.4%).

key_findings.finding: Mephedrone was quantified in 38 deaths. Excluding one value over 2000 mg/L as an outlier (n=37): mean 1.938 mg/L (range <0.01 to 22.0); 10 'monomephedrone' cases mean 1.996 mg/L (range <0.01 to 12.15); 27 combined cases mean 1.749 mg/L (range 0.03 to 22.0). The specimen is named only as post-mortem blood, in the Discussion; sampling site, time after death and method are not reported, and there is no comparison with deaths from other causes or living people; the discussion calls the mean blood levels broadly in line with earlier small, anecdotal reports.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph (p. 711, right column, continuing at the top of p. 712, left column); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 712)
key_findings.note: The PDF's text layer renders the outlier as '92000 mg/L'; the printed page reads '>2000 mg/L' (checked on 300- and 500-dpi renderings). The three means are mutually inconsistent (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The authors say a non-negligible share of alleged 'mephedrone fatalities' turned out not to be related to the substance because other drugs were identified at post-mortem, and relate this to media interest and public concern about mephedrone's rapid appearance; they say confirmed deaths seemed to fall gradually after the spring 2010 classification process, and that the weekend excess fits recreational use.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In the polydrug deaths, the authors say mephedrone's precise role remains unclear; they read the minority of mephedrone-only deaths as possibly confirming concern about its own acute toxicity, and offer untested explanations for the combinations found (stimulants to maintain arousal, sedatives or opioids to modulate effects).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors call self-harm, especially hanging, the mechanism of death in almost 30% of inquests, with risky behaviour in 6 more (9.7%); note that full psychiatric histories are not usually available to np-SAD; report few antipsychotic and antidepressant findings and 'no apparent differences' between intentional and non-intentional deaths (no data shown); raise the possibility that mephedrone causes or worsens psychosis or depression; and contrast suicide rates of 3% to 6% recorded by UK coroners in larger series on amphetamine-type drugs, MDMA, cocaine and khat.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 712, right column, continuing on p. 713, left column)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: some positive cases await inquiry or inquest; mephedrone's presence in post-mortem toxicology does not necessarily mean it caused or contributed to death; changes over time may reflect changes in coroners' methods, policies, laws or forensic technology; given test sensitivity and specificity, failure to detect mephedrone should be interpreted with caution, so the count is likely an underestimate; environmental triggers (overcrowding, heat) were not analysed; coverage of coroners' jurisdictions and of prescribing is incomplete; concentrations are missing for some deaths; and without a death rate per occasion of use the size of the risk cannot be determined.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says antipsychotics were found in 8 deaths and antidepressants in 5; the Results and Table 2 give antidepressants 8 and antipsychotics 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two counts are swapped in the Discussion's argument about psychiatric medication; cite Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall mean concentration (1.938 mg/L, n=37) cannot be the combination of the subgroup means: (10 × 1.996 + 27 × 1.749) / 37 = 1.816 mg/L (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the three means, or the subgroup sizes, is wrong; none of the means can be relied on to the third decimal.

reporting_issues.issue: Ten 'monomephedrone' concentration cases are reported, but mephedrone was the only substance found in only 8 deaths; 'monomephedrone' is not defined (it might mean mephedrone alone in the cause of death, 18 deaths).
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison of mephedrone-only with combined cases cannot be interpreted.

reporting_issues.issue: The number employed is printed as 'Many' followed by a superscript 24, which points to reference 24 (a paper on mephedrone myths and mass information), not to a count.
reporting_issues.consequence: The employment count is unknown; if it was 24, then 24 + 18 + 11 = 53 and 9 are unaccounted for (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion describe typical victims as male, but the number of men and women is never given (only their mean ages).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex distribution cannot be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 1 gives 128 overall deaths, but the monthly labels of the suspected-death series sum to 123 (editors' reading); the series 'caused or contributed to by mephedrone' sums to 35, against 36 deaths with mephedrone formally in the cause of death in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: There is a five-count discrepancy between the suspected-series labels and the stated total, and a one-count discrepancy between the causal series and the text. Missing dates, plotting errors or other explanations cannot be distinguished from the paper; do not repair the monthly series or assert that exactly five distinct deaths were omitted.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table 2 says one of the 62 'confirmed' deaths had no mephedrone at post-mortem (the person died in hospital 3 weeks after taking it), while the Results describe the 62 as drawn from the 90 deaths with mephedrone identified at post-mortem.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Results' post-mortem-positive definition is not uniform across the 62. An earlier finding or history could explain the delayed hospital death, but its individual confirmation evidence is not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls 95% np-SAD's 'average annual response rate'; the Methods say 95% of coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly; no case-level completeness is given, and none for Scotland, Northern Ireland or the Islands.
reporting_issues.consequence: The completeness of the UK-wide count is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that alcohol may increase mephedrone's effects is supported by references 26 and 27, whose titles concern MDMA (immune response in people using MDMA; ecstasy and polydrug death rates), not mephedrone.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper gives no evidence on alcohol with mephedrone; no claim about that combination should rest on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors' grouping counts 18 deaths from self-inflicted harm (Table 1), while the coroners' or procurators fiscal's verdicts include 11 suicides and 8 open verdicts (Results, 2nd paragraph); the paper does not say how its grouping relates to the legal verdicts.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion's figure of almost 30% self-harm rests on the authors' own classification of the circumstances, not on the recorded verdicts; how many of the 18 had a suicide verdict is unknown.
